evidence: SEC ended its legal defense of the 2024 climate disclosure rule in March 2025 under Acting Chair Mark Uyeda, then formally proposed full rescission on 29 May 2026; Atkins called the rule 'a dramatic overreach.' The public comment period closed 3 Aug 2026. As of late Nov 2026, the Commission has not yet held a final rescission vote; coverage expects one in late 2026 or early 2027, with the exact date still unscheduled.
source: sec.gov; ballotpedia.org; daypitney.com; duanemorris.com; ballotpedia.org (Oct-Nov 2026 status coverage)
strategic_recommendation: Deprioritize SEC-rule-specific compliance spend; formal rescission is already proposed. Redirect that budget toward California SB253/SB261 and EU reporting obligations, which are moving the opposite direction.

key_actors: Chair Andrew Ferguson (Trump-appointed); FTC rulemaking staff (revision pending since Dec 2022)
evidence: The Green Guides revision has been pending since Dec 2022 and remains unrevised as of 2026; the change in presidential administration (Biden to Trump) came and went with no update; an FTC spokesperson said in Jan 2025 there was 'nothing new to share.' Consistent with Ferguson's stated 'enforcement over rulemaking' posture. But this does not mean lighter-touch treatment in practice: enforcement under the existing, unrevised guides has tightened through 2024-2025, with carbon-neutral, biodegradable, and unqualified-recyclability claims all triggering real consent decrees. Net effect: the text isn't moving, but enforcement risk under it is not relaxing either; the same 'stable but with a real countervailing dynamic' pattern as UK_pEPR below Reconfirmed as of fall 2026: still no update to the Green Guides text since the Dec 2022 review reopened; the 2012 guides remain the operative federal framework.
source: packagingdive.com; theregreview.org; ftc.gov; allaboutadvertisinglaw.com (Nov 2026 status reconfirmation)
strategic_recommendation: Treat the unrevised text as a floor, not a ceiling. Enforcement on carbon-neutral, biodegradable and unqualified-recyclability claims has tightened even without a rule change.

key_actors: Sen. Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco), author; Gov. Gavin Newsom (D)
evidence: Wiener publicly responded to the SEC's rollback saying 'California's climate leadership is more critical than ever'; an explicit statement positioning the state law as a left-state counterweight to federal-right deregulation. Newsom's term-limited exit in Jan 2027 is a real date to re-check this against Update, 9 Nov 2026: the Ninth Circuit let Scope 1-2 disclosure proceed (the 10 Nov 2026 deadline held) but found Scope 3 requirements likely unconstitutional under strict scrutiny and remanded Scope 3 to the district court for a severability and injunctive-relief decision. The core law is not rolled back; Scope 3 specifically is paused pending that remand.
source: sd11.senate.ca.gov; sidley.com; stblaw.com; morganlewis.com (Nov 2026 Ninth Circuit ruling)
strategic_recommendation: The 10 Nov 2026 Scope 1-2 deadline held after the Ninth Circuit let it proceed; treat that reporting as done, not upcoming. Scope 3 is a different story: the same ruling found it likely unconstitutional and sent it back to the district court on severability, so the 2027 Scope 3 start is paused, not cancelled. Keep Scope 3 data collection warm rather than restarting it from zero if the injunction later narrows.

key_actors: Sen. Henry Stern, Sen. Lena Gonzalez (D); same Climate Accountability Package as SB253
evidence: Passed as part of the same 2023 package with the same Democratic authorship and the same 2026 political defense posture as SB253 Update, 9 Nov 2026: the Ninth Circuit reversed the district court and enjoined enforcement outright, holding that SB261 compels disclosures beyond commercial speech and likely violates the First Amendment. This confirms, at the appellate level, what the 18 Nov 2025 posture only anticipated; the authoring coalition's political defense of the law is unchanged, but enforcement is now blocked, not merely paused awaiting appeal.
source: sd11.senate.ca.gov; ga-institute.com; sidley.com; stblaw.com; morganlewis.com; skadden.com (Nov 2026 Ninth Circuit ruling)
strategic_recommendation: The Ninth Circuit's 9 Nov 2026 ruling confirms SB261 enforcement is blocked on First Amendment grounds, not merely paused pending appeal as before. Keep the underlying climate-risk disclosure drafted and ready rather than fully shelving it: the statute itself still exists, the authoring coalition is unlikely to abandon it, and further review (en banc or beyond) is still possible.

key_actors: EPP (largest group) + Patriots for Europe + ECR ('right-wing alliance', per Business & Human Rights Resource Centre reporting)
evidence: The Commission's own simplification review, which the Dec 2025 revision obliged it to carry out by end-April 2026, was published 4 May 2026: a review report, updated Guidance and FAQs, a draft Delegated Act on product scope, and an updated Implementing Act on the Information System, but no further delay. The 30 Dec 2026 large/medium date and 30 Jun 2027 SME date stand firm; the Commission's own framing signals this is a political as well as legal 'no third extension.' This supersedes the prior reading of the end-April review as a live opening for another weakening move.
source: esgtoday.com; business-humanrights.org; consilium.europa.eu; hlc.com; hhc.earth (May 2026 Commission simplification-review coverage)
strategic_recommendation: The Commission's review, concluded 4 May 2026, ruled out a third delay: the 30 Dec 2026 large/medium deadline (and 30 Jun 2027 for SMEs) is now firm, not provisional. Build traceability to that date directly; waiting for another postponement is no longer a reasonable bet.

key_actors: Same EPP + Patriots for Europe + ECR coalition; European Commission (von der Leyen, EPP) proposed the underlying Omnibus I package
evidence: Parliament adopted its Omnibus I negotiating position 382-249-13 (13 Nov 2025); Council gave final approval 24 Feb 2026; entered into force 18 Mar 2026. Confirms the previously-unverified figure in docs/data_sources.md: ESRS mandatory datapoints cut from 1073 to 320 (~70% reduction) Added detail: post-Omnibus, CSRD applies only above 1,000 employees and EUR 450M net turnover (up from 250 employees / EUR 50M), taking roughly 80% of previously-covered companies out of scope.
source: sphera.com; clifford chance 2026-02; eubelius.com; gibsondunn.com (CSRD/CSDDD Omnibus scope-threshold coverage)
strategic_recommendation: Rebuild reporting scope around the leaner, Omnibus-cut ESRS (roughly 320 mandatory datapoints, down from 1073), not the pre-Omnibus standard. Plan data collection toward Wave 2/3 filings from 2028.

key_actors: Same Omnibus I coalition and process as CSRD (single combined package)
evidence: Same vote/timeline as CSRD; CSDDD substantive-requirements scope reduced in the same 382-249-13 Parliament vote and Feb 2026 Council approval Added detail: post-Omnibus, CSDDD applies only above 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net turnover, with substantive requirements starting 2029 as already recorded.
source: sphera.com; business-humanrights.org; gibsondunn.com (CSRD/CSDDD Omnibus scope-threshold coverage)
strategic_recommendation: Confirm whether the business still sits inside the narrowed largest-company scope before continuing due-diligence build-out at pre-Omnibus intensity; substantive requirements now apply from 2029.

key_actors: EPP (European People's Party); sent a formal letter 18 Jun 2025 explicitly requesting withdrawal
evidence: The European Commission announced its intent to withdraw the Green Claims Directive proposal on 20 Jun 2025; two days after an EPP letter (18 Jun 2025) explicitly called for withdrawal, citing requirements that were 'overly complex, administratively burdensome, and costly.' The same EPP-led simplification pattern that also produced the Omnibus I (CSRD/CSDDD) outcome and the second EUDR delay, now landing on a fourth file. Status remains technically unresolved; the Commission has not formally terminated the proposal, and Parliament committee chairs have signaled readiness to resume negotiations, so a revival isn't ruled out. The separate, already-adopted EmpCo directive is unaffected and proceeds on its own track (see the EmpCo row below)
strategic_recommendation: Don't deprioritize green-claims substantiation work on the strength of this withdrawal announcement; the proposal hasn't been formally terminated, and EmpCo already covers much of the same ground regardless.

key_actors: European Commission (infringement enforcement); 20 lagging member states including Belgium, Spain, France, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal
evidence: EmpCo (Directive (EU) 2024/825) is a separate, already-adopted directive from the withdrawn Green Claims Directive proposal above; it is not being weakened. Member states had until 27 Mar 2026 to transpose it into national law; on 28 May 2026 the Commission opened infringement procedures (letters of formal notice) against 20 member states for failing to do so. The rules become binding EU-wide from 27 Sep 2026 regardless of transposition status in the laggard states. Germany and Italy, among others, had fully transposed it as of June 2026. This is a member-state administrative-compliance-lag story, not a left/right ideological vote; marked 'mixed' rather than forced onto a left/right axis Update, as of 8 Oct 2026: 19 of 27 member states now have EmpCo laws in force (up from the handful confirmed in the original pass), one has passed legislation awaiting signature, five have drafts or bills in progress, and two have not yet put forward a measure. The 27 Sep 2026 EU-wide binding date applies regardless of each state's own transposition progress.
source: climatepartner.com; cms.law implementation tracker; xictron.com; freshfields.com EmpCo transposition tracker (Oct 2026)
strategic_recommendation: Comply to the 27 Sep 2026 EU-wide binding date directly, rather than to any single member state's transposition status; the directive applies even where local transposition is still lagging.

key_actors: European Parliament (426 in favour, 125 against, 74 abstentions, adopted Nov 2024); Council final adoption Dec 2024
evidence: PPWR passed with a broad cross-party majority (426-125-74); well before the 2025-2026 EPP-led simplification wave that later hit CSRD/CSDDD/EUDR/Green Claims. It entered into force 11 Feb 2025 and applies from 12 Aug 2026 as already scheduled, with recycled-content grading phasing in from 2030. Widely reported as 'the most lobbied political process in the EU's history' during drafting, but the final vote margin shows it wasn't a narrow ideological win the way the later Omnibus-era votes were. Worth re-checking once it's actually in force and post-application lobbying resumes, but no active simplification push was found this pass Update: application proceeded on schedule 12 Aug 2026 despite Czechia leading a group of member states that lobbied for a delay via the 25 Jun 2026 Environment Council agenda; the date did not move. As of 5 Nov 2026, two delegated acts are adopted (pallet wrappings and straps; crystal glass packaging) out of roughly 30 expected over the coming years; the labelling implementing act, originally expected for Aug 2026, has slipped to Q4 2026.
source: howtheyvote.eu vote 168504; foodpackagingforum.org; europen-packaging.eu; erp-recycling.org; europen-packaging.eu (PPWR secondary-legislation tracker, Nov 2026)
strategic_recommendation: This is the one EU packaging rule the 2025-2026 simplification wave hasn't touched. Treat its 12 Aug 2026 application date and 2030 recycled-content phase-in as fixed, and prioritize packaging investment here over EUDR- or CSRD-adjacent bets.

key_actors: Defra Secretary Dame Angela Eagle (Labour, appointed 20 Jul 2026 under PM Burnham)
evidence: Packaging EPR is proceeding into its planned fee-modulation phase for 2026 as scheduled; continuity from the framework Labour inherited from the prior Conservative government. But Defra separately postponed mandatory kerbside soft-plastics collection from 2027 to 2030, showing delay pressure exists even under a nominally pro-regulation government, most likely administrative-burden/cost driven rather than a partisan reversal Confirmed rates for 2026-27: Red-rated (hard-to-recycle) packaging pays a 1.2x multiplier on the base fee, rising to 1.6x in 2027-28 and 2.0x in 2028-29; illustrative 2026-27 plastic-packaging fees run about £415/tonne for Green-rated packaging versus £545/tonne for Red-rated.
source: erp-recycling.org; grantthornton.co.uk; hansard.parliament.uk 2026-07-01; ecosurety.com; xeliport.com (2026-27 confirmed EPR fee schedule)
strategic_recommendation: Budget now for the October 2026 fee eco-modulation change. The separate postponement of mandatory kerbside soft-plastics collection (2027 to 2030) doesn't relax the fee timeline.

key_actors: HM Treasury (no named political controversy identified)
evidence: Rate rises automatically each April in line with CPI inflation (now £228.82/tonne from 1 Apr 2026); no partisan dispute or reversal found
strategic_recommendation: Model the recycled-content threshold as a recurring, CPI-indexed cost (now £228.82/tonne from April 2026), not a one-off tax line. No political reversal is in view.
